title: Number of Boomerangs
spaceBreakdown:
- unordered_map<long long,int> cnt: up to n−1 entries per center iteration, reused → O(n)
- recursion depth: none
- not counted: input vector, returned int
approach: For each point i (the "center"), count how many other points share each squared distance from i. If c points are at the same distance, they form c·(c−1) ordered (j, k) pairs (order matters, so permutations not combinations). Sum over all centers and all distance groups. Using squared distance avoids floating-point issues and keeps everything in integers.
hints: For a fixed point i, what property must points j and k share for (i, j, k) to be a boomerang? The constraint n ≤ 500 means an O(n²) approach is affordable.
Use a hash map keyed by squared distance from the center point i. In Example 1, fixing i = [1,0], both [0,0] and [2,0] land at squared distance 1, yielding 2 ordered (j, k) pairs.

**Order matters** - the tuple (i, j, k) is ordered, so (j, k) and (k, j) are distinct.
`Input: [[0,0],[1,0],[2,0]]` → `Expected: 2`
⚠️ Bug: using c*(c-1)/2 instead of c*(c-1) → returns 1

**Inner loop from i+1** - every point j ≠ i must be considered, not just those after i.
`Input: [[0,0],[1,0],[2,0]]` → `Expected: 2`
⚠️ Bug: inner loop `for j = i+1 to n` instead of `for j = 0 to n` → returns 0

**Wrong distance metric** - the problem uses Euclidean distance; Manhattan distance produces false equalities.
`Input: [[0,0],[1,1],[2,0]]` → `Expected: 2`
⚠️ Bug: using |dx|+|dy| instead of dx²+dy² → returns 6

**All equidistant from center** - a single center can contribute many boomerangs from one distance group.
`Input: [[0,0],[1,0],[0,1],[-1,0],[0,-1]]` → `Expected: 20`
⚠️ Bug: using c*(c-1)/2 → returns 10

followUps.q: If coordinates can be up to 10^9, how does the solution change?
followUps.a: Squared distance becomes up to (2×10^9)² = 4×10^18, which exceeds int and even risks int64 overflow when summing two terms - use long long for dx, dy, and d. The algorithm structure stays the same; TC remains O(n²), SC O(n).

followUps.q: If n can be up to 10^5, how would you reduce the O(n²) cost?
followUps.a: This is an open research-style problem; exact counting for all centers is inherently O(n²) in the worst case. An approximate approach could sample centers or use spatial partitioning (e.g., a grid or k-d tree) to prune far-away points, trading accuracy for speed.

followUps.q: If points arrive as a stream and you must answer after each insertion, how would you adapt?
followUps.a: Maintain a hash map per existing center keyed by squared distance. On inserting a new point p, for each existing center i compute d(i, p) and add the current count at that distance to the running total, then increment. TC per insertion is O(n), SC O(n²) total across all centers' maps.
